action_criteria.rationale: A first convulsion in the emergency department warrants a check for hypoglycemia and electrolyte disturbance; nothing in the history points to a provoked seizure, so the test is not essential.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform LP without specific clinical indication.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not pursue cardiac workup as the primary etiology in a patient with classic temporal aura.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for efficacy and tolerability; neither interacts with omeprazole.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Give seizure safety advice (showers rather than baths, no swimming alone, no work at heights) and advise regular sleep and limited alcohol.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, back to baseline within 30 minutes, no meningism and not immunosuppressed: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
No murmur, exertional event or cardiac history, and the semiology is epileptic: echocardiography has no indication.
Aura, automatisms and 30 minutes of postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.
Back to baseline with a normal examination, no head injury and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left mesial temporal lobe origin with hippocampal sclerosis (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with classic mesial-temporal aura)

differential.diagnosis: First unprovoked seizure of unknown etiology
differential.key_features: Excluded: the stereotyped auras of the past six months are prior focal seizures, and the MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis.
No postural prodrome; aura, automatisms, 90 seconds of convulsion and 30 minutes of postictal confusion; normal ECG.
Adult onset without myoclonus, a focal aura and focal left temporal discharges without generalized spike-wave argue against it.
No sleep deprivation, illness or drug change; glucose, sodium and calcium normal and urine drug screen negative.
Stereotyped aura with witnessed tonic-clonic activity is not PNES.

key_clinical_evidence: Three to four stereotyped deja vu and rising epigastric auras in the six months before the convulsion are prior focal seizures, so the two-unprovoked-seizure criterion for epilepsy is met [ILAE_def_2014].
Mesial temporal aura, left hippocampal sclerosis on the epilepsy-protocol MRI and left anterior temporal sharp waves on EEG are concordant.
Right-hand fumbling automatisms are usually ipsilateral to the seizure onset; localization rests on the concordant MRI and EEG [Lateralization_2005].
Childhood febrile seizures are a recognized antecedent of hippocampal sclerosis.
First-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy is lamotrigine or levetiracetam [NICE_NG217_2025]; lamotrigine was more effective than levetiracetam in SANAD II [SANAD2_2021].

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Hernandez is a 34-year-old right-handed male physical therapist who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His wife reports that approximately six hours prior to arrival, she observed the patient suddenly stop mid-conversation and stare blankly for about 10 to 15 seconds. He appeared to smack his lips and fumble with his shirt buttons with his right hand. She called his name but he did not respond. He then developed stiffening of all four extremities followed by rhythmic bilateral jerking lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Following the episode, he was confused and drowsy for approximately 30 minutes before gradually returning to his baseline.

Upon interview, the patient recalls that just before the event he experienced an intense feeling of deja vu accompanied by a peculiar rising sensation from his epigastrium toward his throat. He describes having had similar brief episodes of deja vu with the epigastric rising sensation approximately three to four times over the past six months, each lasting 30 to 60 seconds, after which he would feel momentarily disoriented. He attributed these episodes to stress and did not seek medical attention. He denies any prior convulsions or loss of consciousness other than the febrile seizures in early childhood documented in his medical records. There has been no recent illness, fever, head trauma, sleep deprivation, or changes in medications. He denies any preceding headache, visual changes, or weakness. He has never taken antiepileptic medications.
